analysis.one_liner: Bans forced arbitration clauses in employment, consumer, franchise, and civil rights contracts, restoring access to court.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 118 cosponsors but never received a committee or floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Companies routinely require workers and consumers to sign away their right to sue, sending any dispute to a private arbitrator instead of a judge or jury. This bill would make those pre-dispute arbitration clauses unenforceable for employment, consumer, franchise, and civil rights disputes, and would put a court rather than the arbitrator in charge of deciding whether an arbitration agreement is valid.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers, consumers, franchisees, and civil rights claimants who would otherwise be locked out of court. They regain the right to take disputes before a judge or jury, including the right to join class actions that arbitration clauses commonly bar.

how_it_helps.text: Declares that no pre-dispute arbitration agreement is valid or enforceable if it requires arbitration of an employment, consumer, or franchise dispute, or of a civil rights claim.

Provides that a court, not an arbitrator, decides whether an agreement to arbitrate is valid or enforceable under federal law, closing a route companies used to have the arbitrator rubber-stamp the company's own clause.
Applies to any dispute or claim arising after enactment, so future disputes would go to court while the right to sue is restored going forward.

analysis.who_pays: Large employers, banks, credit card issuers, franchisors, and other consumer-facing corporations that rely on arbitration clauses to keep disputes out of court and out of class actions. They would face litigation costs, and arbitration providers would lose the repeat business those clauses generate.

drawbacks.text: The bill exempts arbitration provisions in collective bargaining agreements, so arbitration can remain the forum for unionized workers if their contract provides for it.
The bill applies only prospectively to disputes arising after enactment, so it would not reopen cases already sent to arbitration.

The strongest good-faith objection: arbitration can be faster and cheaper than court for some individuals, and businesses argue that forcing every dispute into litigation would raise costs. The bill's own findings counter that the arbitration system was designed for disputes between businesses of similar power, not consumers and employees, and that clauses are often buried in fine print people never knowingly agreed to.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary people the bill removes a system that, per its findings, strips their day in court as a condition of jobs, credit cards, and everyday purchases. The cost falls on corporations that would again face courtrooms and class actions. The design is clean but modest in one respect: it does nothing for disputes already arbitraged, and it leaves collectively bargained arbitration in place.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Judiciary Committee for nearly two years; its subcommittee was discharged but the full committee never voted on it, and the Congress ended without a floor vote.

narrative.text: Hank Johnson of Georgia introduced the bill on February 12, 2009, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the same day.
On March 16, 2009 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Commercial and Administrative Law, and on June 21, 2010 that subcommittee was discharged.

The bill grew to 118 cosponsors, including 117 of the 253 House Democrats and a single House Republican, but the full Judiciary Committee never reported it and the House never voted on it before the Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations that use mandatory arbitration clauses to keep employment and consumer disputes out of court, and the arbitration firms whose business those clauses feed. A majority of the House's majority party cosponsored the bill, but the committee it sat in never acted on it.

for.name: Hank Johnson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited a broad slate of original cosponsors.

for.name: 1 of 178 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only Republican to do so.

against.name: John Conyers
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee that received the bill; it was discharged from subcommittee in June 2010 but never received a committee vote, markup, or floor action.

against.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce
against.what_they_did: Opposed bills banning mandatory arbitration and defended the enforceability of forced arbitration clauses in employment and consumer contracts.

sides.party_line_note: 117 of 253 House Democrats cosponsored the bill against just 1 of 178 House Republicans, and no vote was ever taken.

industries.note: Their lucrative repeat business comes from corporations that require millions of consumers and employees to arbitrate; the bill voids those mandatory clauses. The bill's findings note these firms face pressure to favor the corporate repeat players who decide whether they get the business.

They would lose the ability to require workers and customers to sign away court access as a condition of a job, a credit card, or a purchase, and would face lawsuits and class actions they currently avoid.
Franchise disputes would no longer be forced into arbitration under pre-dispute clauses, giving franchisees access to court.
Restored access to court and class actions creates work for lawyers representing individuals, whose interest here runs alongside the workers and consumers they would represent.
